Hims & Hers launches latest peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S.
  • Even as it revealed the latest products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.
  • Sources indicate that the new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday said it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it revealed the latest products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

Sources indicate that the new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October introduced an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a company spokesperson mentioned in a statement.

None of the company's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims said they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy.".

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

The company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

It has been revealed that hims stated it prepares to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The company also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized plan to their needs, if appropriate.

The company said it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

"If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options.".

However, Vinjamoori mentioned there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

Industry observers note that "We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he said. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a company of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead.".

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He said Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight.".

According to recent reports, but health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," stated Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body.".

Kritzer said the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Recent findings suggest that without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, stated Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide people, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler mentioned one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

In a recent development, "With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?".

According to recent reports, but he said the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

That appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The firm says patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that says the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

According to recent reports, HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "big fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

There is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data highlights only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione revealed that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also said in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

Sources indicate that all of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR).
  • The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer new clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.

The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.

Until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.

A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses.

The newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.

Industry observers note that despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.

Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.

The latest discovery provides an notable breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.

It has been revealed that "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," said lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.

McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.

To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away.

The radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.

In a recent development, according to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.

The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface.".

A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.

The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.

"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.".

Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair.

ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.

The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.

According to recent reports, "We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," noted Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

Sources indicate that after the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.

The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.

The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.

According to recent reports, both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.

For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.

Recent findings suggest that dr. McSweeney said, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.".

The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion.".

#1105. Breaking: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1702 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that while we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • In a recent development, the findings raise important questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But new research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

In a recent development, the findings raise important questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

"We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," notes Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

The study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

According to recent reports, deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

Recent findings suggest that in 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an key role in carrying away waste products.

Recent findings suggest that that earlier discovery led to a new question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

It has been revealed that previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially notable.

To investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

According to recent reports, each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

According to recent reports, the researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

Recent findings suggest that the results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings indicated that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

It has been revealed that the researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

Industry observers note that when a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

It has been revealed that to measure this response, the researchers revealed volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

Industry observers note that in many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Recent findings suggest that participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Once again, the older group showed a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

Using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

"Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes says. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have crucial implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

Recent findings suggest that none of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants demonstrated signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

Sources indicate that the relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

Sources indicate that in a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

While older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

Sources indicate that "It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis states. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

#1102. A newly introduced approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine indicates early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1475 w)

A newly introduced approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine indicates early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

It has been revealed that china and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

Recent findings suggest that the US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

Industry observers note that as long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, claims study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

Sources indicate that the immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler said.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with latest variants.

The latest nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

Sources indicate that the researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

According to recent reports, “You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

Recent findings suggest that as promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

Industry observers note that “They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, noted Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the newly introduced research.

It has been revealed that the study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an upgrade.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler claims they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss firm called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Recent findings suggest that other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland mentioned. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In reality, Poland mentioned, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he noted.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team notes it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very key in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

In a recent development, they have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

FluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Sources indicate that another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

The creative, whose film The Frozen Fire was Sri Lanka’s first-ever submission for the best international feature film Oscar, soon got involved with the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), whose 30th edition wraps up this weekend, and its Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event (ITBE) market. Gunathilake notes it is all about building bridges. And that goes beyond the bridges and networks that socializing and discussing the craft naturally creates. “There is a gap between academia and the film industry,” he tells THR. “We thought it is a responsibility of film festivals to help bridge industry and academia and bring them together.”.

Sources indicate that case in point: Students fresh out of film schools, whether focused on cinematography or other areas, “may have never heard of a sales agent and what they do, they don’t know what distribution is and they have never heard of a subject called audience study,” he explains. “So we thought it would be very interesting to introduce this ecosystem of the afterlife of the film when they make one? What actually happens to this film?”.

It has been revealed that gunathilake states beyond general education, mentorship is a key focus for him and his team. “It is important to create a platform where mentors are coming – big filmmakers – and emerging talents can present their film and have an exchange with them. They can come together and sit and talk and discuss.”.

It has been revealed that the feedback on these opportunities is strong to enthusiastic. For example, one younger cinematographer from Spain got to spend time with the acclaimed Roberto Schaefer (Finding Neverland, Monster’s Ball, Quantum of Solace). “She mentioned that she never thought she could sit at a breakfast table and talk about her film with Roberto,” Gunathilake tells THR. “And Roberto had seen her film, and then they could talk.”.

The importance of mentoring is actually captured in the official motto of the Discovery Campus that is featured on its website: “Learn from the mistakes of our mentors, so you don’t have to make them yourself!”.

Among the significant industry names who have shared their insights and tips at Tallinn this year are the likes of Sentimental Value casting director Yngvill Haga, Julio Macat, the cinematographer behind the likes of Miracle on 34th Street and Home Alone, and dual screenplay Oscar winner Christopher Hampton.

Breaking: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary.
  • According to recent reports, now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds.
  • The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary. Unlike Earth, which has a relatively orderly magnetic field with clearly defined north and south poles, both distant planets possess strangely distorted and dramatically tilted magnetic fields. For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why.

According to recent reports, now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds. A latest study suggests that changes in how well materials conduct electricity under extreme conditions could explain the planets' unusual magnetism. The findings also raise an intriguing possibility: the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may change dramatically over just a few decades.

The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.

Why Uranus and Neptune Have Such Strange Magnetic Fields.

Sources indicate that planetary magnetic fields originate deep beneath the surface, where moving fluids capable of conducting electricity generate magnetic forces. Scientists call this process a dynamo.

Sources indicate that on Earth, the dynamo operates within the outer core, a layer of molten metal surrounded by mostly solid rock. As liquid iron circulates and the planet rotates, it generates a magnetic field resembling that of a giant bar magnet. This produces the familiar north and south magnetic poles that allow compasses to point in a consistent direction.

Earth's magnetic field is also closely aligned with its rotation axis. Its main magnetic axis, known as a dipole, is tilted by only 11 degrees. Uranus and Neptune are strikingly different. Uranus has a magnetic dipole tilted by 59 degrees, while Neptune's is tilted by 47 degrees.

Explaining these extreme tilts requires a better understanding of what lies inside the two planets.

It has been revealed that uranus and Neptune are classified as ice giants, a name that reflects their presumed composition rather than suggesting they are simply frozen worlds. Each is approximately four times wider than Earth, and scientists believe their interiors contain substantial amounts of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rocky material. However, their precise internal compositions remain uncertain.

Extreme Conditions Deep Inside the Ice Giants.

Chi Yan, the study's lead author and a research associate at the UT Jackson School of Geosciences, believes the combination of the planets' enormous size and unusual chemical makeup may help explain their distorted magnetic fields.

Recent findings suggest that "Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," remarked Yan. "Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.".

In a recent development, ions are electrically charged particles that can carry electric current. If the materials inside Uranus and Neptune become more conductive at greater depths, that could significantly influence how their magnetic fields are generated.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed computer simulations designed to reproduce the strange magnetic fields recorded by Voyager 2.

According to recent reports, their models assumed that electrical conductivity increases deeper inside the planets. The researchers also tested a variety of possible internal structures, examining how circulating fluids, temperature changes, and magnetic forces interact over time.

The results suggest that these changing electrical properties could play a crucial role in producing the unusual magnetic fields observed around both ice giants.

Magnetic Poles Could Shift Dramatically Within Decades.

Perhaps the most surprising finding is that the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may be far less stable than Earth's.

Industry observers note that according to the simulations, their magnetic axes could undergo substantial changes in relatively short periods. In some scenarios, the magnetic tilt shifted by tens of degrees within only a few decades.

That raises the possibility that the magnetic fields surrounding Uranus and Neptune today are significantly different from those measured when Voyager 2 flew past them in the 1980s.

"Earth's magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," stated Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.".

It has been revealed that these dramatic changes remain predictions from computer models rather than confirmed observations. However, scientists may already have a way to look for evidence of them.

James Webb Telescope Could Reveal Magnetic Changes.

Researchers are now examining detailed infrared images of Uranus and Neptune captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They are particularly interested in the planets' auroras, which form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in their atmospheres.

Auroras are closely connected to planetary magnetic fields, making them valuable clues to what is happening far above the planets' hidden interiors. Changes in the appearance and arrangement of these glowing atmospheric features could help researchers determine whether the magnetic poles have shifted since Voyager 2's encounters.

"We are busy working on what's contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere, promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an key stepping stone," said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign and reviewed the paper for the journal.

The ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing electrically charged particles. Its behavior is influenced by magnetic activity, offering another potential source of information about the planets' changing magnetic environments.

The research team hopes to combine Webb's auroral observations with Voyager 2's original magnetic field measurements and the newly introduced dynamo simulations. Together, these sources of evidence could provide the clearest picture yet of how the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are arranged today.

Recent findings suggest that even so, scientists emphasize that fully understanding the planets' deep interiors will require fresh spacecraft missions to these distant worlds. Until then, improved simulations and powerful telescopes may help unravel one of the solar system's most unusual magnetic mysteries.

The research was funded by The University of Texas Institute for Geophysics (UTIG) in the Jackson School of Geosciences, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and the Science and Technology Facilities Council.

It has been revealed that rüfüs Du Sol‘s emotional banger “Innerbloom” is well-established dance world canon, having provided the soundtrack to weddings, anniversaries, birthdays, engagements and other extra special moments since its release on Nov. 20, 2015 — eleven years ago today.

Today (Nov. 20) the already epic track becomes even more so under the watch of legend Hans Zimmer, who’s just released his take on the song in collaboration with Rüfüs du Sol and Bleeding Fingers, the scoring collective Zimmer co-founded to make music for films.

This version, “Innerbloom XI,” maintains the nine-minute length of the original, but takes the song to Zimmer’s characteristically sweeping cinematic scale, adding strings, percussion, xylophone, a choir and layers (and layers) of other instrumentation that makes the song fit squarely among Zimmer’s unparalleled Academy Award-winning body of work.

“Innerbloom XI” is accompanied by a new film from Rüfüs’s longtime creative director Katzki, made in collaboration with visual artist Thomás Blanchard that recreates the music video for the original. Watch the “Innerbloom XI” music video below.

Coming from Rüfüs’ du Sol’s second album, 2016’s Bloom, “Innerbloom” has generated 290 million official on-demand U.S. streams and a billion official on-demand global streams, according to Luminate. The song was a major highlight of the group’s recent Inhale/Exhale tour, a global two-year run that became nothing less than the biggest electronic tour of all time.

Industry observers note that beyond this “Innerbloom XI” project, upcoming music from Zimmer will next be heard in the third installment of the Dune franchise, which is in theaters Dec. 18.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hollywood is mourning a marvelous talent.

It has been revealed that lance Broadway, the former pitcher for the Chicago White Sox and Fresh York Mets, died unexpectedly on Nov. 17, according to the Dallas County Medical Examiner's Office. He was 43.

In a recent development, the Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. actor died in an apartment complex stairwell in Dallas, Texas, public records confirm, though his cause of death is still pending autopsy results.

Broadway began his career in the spotlight with the Chicago baseball team when he was selected as the 15th overall pick at the 2005 MLB draft.

He spent two years in Triple-A—the highest level in Minor League Baseball—before making his Major League debut in 2007 as the White Sox's third-best prospect.

According to recent reports, the Sox ultimately traded him to the New York Mets for Ramón Castro two years later. After a few months back in the minors, he was called up to take over for Óliver Perez. But his time on the field didn't end in NYC. Broadway signed with the Toronto Blue Jays three months later to a minor-league deal, concluding his MLB career after a full season with the Triple-A Las Vegas 51s.

Though the former athlete threw his final pitch in 2010, he wasn't ready to bid farewell to the camera just yet. In fact, he went on to make his acting debut in 2011's Deadly Notes and Food Attack.

He then went on to star in Olympus Has Fallen (2013) as Agent O'Neil and played a TAC Team Leader in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.

Broadway previously revealed that transitioning to acting after concluding his professional sports career wasn't a total surprise.

"It's been a wild ride, that's for sure," he told Screen Slam in 2013. "2010 was my last season and in every offseason I wanted to get involved with something. And I don't know why, but I just wanted to go take an improv class.".

"The improv class I wanted didn't start until January 2011, so I asked a friend who told me to go take an acting class," he recalled. "That way, at least I will be in front of people doing something while they watch. So I got into an acting class in November 2010. I loved it and stuck with it.".

Broadway emphasized that his past experience in sports stayed with him in his new career, especially when he worked with Gerard Butler, Aaron Eckhart and Morgan Freeman on Olympus Has Fallen.

Industry observers note that "It was the same feeling as walking into a substantial-league locker room with guys that you knew were established, had earned the right to speak, and you do not have that right," he recalled. "I learned so much from these actors and everyone was so nice, but I was just watching them go about their business.”.

“I did the same thing in the major leagues,” he added. “I remember the first time I was called up to Chicago, I just wanted to watch and see how these guys went about doing everything.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.

This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.

“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded. “Killed by women.”.

Sources indicate that in case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.

“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.

Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.

It has been revealed that the concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.).

More frustrated responses to the massively popular GTA VI came from looksmaxxing influencer Braden Peters, aka Clavicular, (the game required too much “simping for girls,” the streamer, at the moment facing multiple rape charges, complained on X), anti-woke gamer activist Mark Kern, aka Grummz (he called the housework “mundane crap”), and misinformation superspreader Dom Lucre, who falsely claimed that Rockstar had specifically made it impossible to open fire in a gay nightclub. (Washington Post critic Gene Park pointed out that the club in question was not LGBTQ-specific and that the mechanics of the game don’t allow you to shoot anyone in any kind of club.) These comments came alongside the predictable gripes over supposedly “overweight” female characters with insufficiently large breasts.

If the Tates, incels, and other far-right reactionaries of the world are so bent out of shape, it’s probably because whereas GTA once punched down at marginalized groups like sex workers and transgender people, bigots and self-styled alpha males are now the butt of the joke. The Vice City of GTA VI is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout MAGA-coded conspiracy theories and call you a “libtard” or “commie socialist” if you walk into them. These touches seem to have made the game into “a bug zapper for chuds,” as one Bluesky user put it. (That hasn’t stopped Republicans and Trump allies from trying and failing to score political points with the game.).

Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element of GTA VI.

It’s not that games like The Sims haven’t explored this territory before, and Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption franchise paid similar attention to quotidian detail. In those frontier-set narratives, your cowboy character had to make coffee over campfires and even clean up manure in barns. By addressing characters’ most basic needs—you can even manage personal hygiene by showering—GTA VI recalls some of the slower and quieter aspects of that franchise.

What’s truly remarkable, though, is that adult men who grew up indulging their most selfish and sociopathic instincts in the older GTA games have had their nostalgia for those escapades cleverly complicated with real-life problems. They can still steal cars, sell drugs, and rise through the ranks of a seedy underworld. That will always be the appeal of the series, which is now asking eternally aggrieved culture warriors to consider a vital question: What if you didn’t have to do it alone?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19). They will discuss the future of the Eastern European country that has been under attack from Russia since February 2022 and is now facing yet another harsh winter.

In a recent development, extensive security measures have already been confirmed for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants. It remains unclear whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be among them. What does appear certain, however, is the attendance of chief US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, according to several media outlets.

Industry observers note that the "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack. Unlike other international forums, the group is focused not only on how to support Ukraine militarily and financially in the here and now.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, led by Germany, France and the United Kingdom, the coalition is also prepared, in principle, to help monitor a possible ceasefire within Ukraine itself and to contribute to the complex security guarantees the country would then require, should such a scenario come to pass. The effort dates back to March 2025, when the countries involved first met in London.

In a recent development, but what can the coalition realistically achieve? Stefan Meister of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) is not overly optimistic.

In a recent development, "The fundamental problem is that Europe has yet to put forward a proposal," he told DW. "There is no strategy outlining what security guarantees Europe would offer, what troops it would be prepared to deploy, what measures it could provide to safeguard a ceasefire, or where it would be willing to make compromises.".

According to recent reports, nevertheless, the meeting comes at a moment when some observers believe there may finally be movement toward ending the war. During talks in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates a few days ago, Russia, Ukraine and the US managed to agree only on a prisoner exchange. It was a modest step forward.

Further talks are planned, and it has been a long time since the prospects appeared as favorable as they do now for Europe to secure a role in future decisions on war and peace in Ukraine.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has repeatedly been argued, both by US officials and by those in power in Russia, that Europe does not speak with a single voice.

In a recent development, this has sparked a debate among EU heads of state and government over who, exactly, could represent Europe in such talks. Could it be German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)?

After the EU summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Friday, Merz mentioned: "For the first time, concrete peace talks are expected to take place in the coming weeks with Europe represented. Germany has a seat at the table, that is absolutely clear.".

But what exactly did that mean? That Germany alone would speak for all of Europe? Hardly. As was also made clear in Berlin on Monday, Europe would be represented by the E3 countries, namely Germany, France, and the non-EU member United Kingdom, joined by Poland and Italy. Official EU representatives, including European Council President Antonio Costa, would also take part.

Stefan Meister of the DGAP believes the debate states a great deal about the pressures Europe itself is under.

"Europe's positioning has more to do with domestic political considerations than with developments in the negotiations," Meister mentioned. "Everyone needs to show that they are participating in the talks in some way. Elections will be held next year in France and Poland, and it is still unclear whether French support for Ukraine will continue in its current form after that.".

German Deputy Government Spokesperson Sebastian Hille, meanwhile, sought to downplay the debate on Monday over a possible role for Friedrich Merz as chief negotiator.

At the federal government's regular press briefing, he said: "This is not about discussing individuals. What matters is that Putin finally understands that he must come to the negotiating table so that we have a chance of achieving peace in the first place.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US negotiator Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, struck a rather different tone last week.

Speaking in Abu Dhabi, he noted: "If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.".

Industry observers note that government spokesperson Hille responded on Monday: "Europe's strength lies precisely in the unity and cohesion of many countries. We should not allow ourselves to be drawn into debates that others want to frame around this question.".

Sources indicate that hille emphasized that the situation remained unchanged: Peace in Ukraine could only be achieved step by step. Europe, too, would need stamina, perseverance and a willingness to undertake the painstaking work required to bring it about.

European supporters of Ukraine are also under pressure as public opinion on the problem is shifting, including in Germany. While a broad majority favored helping defend the country in the immediate aftermath of Russia's invasion in the spring of 2022, support has since fallen markedly.

Industry observers note that according to the latest DeutschlandTrend survey on the glitch, conducted or German public broadcaster ARD in September 2026, 52% of eligible voters still support weapons deliveries to Ukraine, while 42% believe such support has gone too far. That is the highest level of opposition recorded since the start of the war.

A further study conducted for public broadcaster WDR in November 2026 found that support for Ukraine has become a more polarizing issue in Germany than immigration. According to the survey, 54% of respondents favor continued support for Ukraine, while just under 29% would prefer a rapprochement with Russia, despite its war of aggression against Ukraine.

#1093. An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an vital difference between human and chimpanzee brain development.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population.
  • Although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an vital difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene that remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in the developing brain.

Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population. They also offer new clues about how the brains of humans and our closest evolutionary relatives may have developed differently.

Although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years. Some of these ancient infections left traces of viral DNA that continue to influence how genes function today.

Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University, states the discovery demonstrates how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population.

"The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is important to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development," states Johan Jakobsson.

How an Ancient Virus Silenced a Brain Development Gene.

Recent findings suggest that at the center of the discovery is a gene called LINC00662. Researchers found that it is active during early human brain development but completely switched off in comparable chimpanzee brain models.

Recent findings suggest that the difference appears to be caused by a genetic remnant of PTERV1, an ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago. PTERV1 belongs to a group known as endogenous retroviruses, which are viruses whose genetic material became incorporated into the DNA of their hosts. Once embedded in the genome, these viral sequences can be inherited by future generations.

According to recent reports, over time, PTERV1 produced numerous copies of its genetic material that became scattered across different parts of the chimpanzee genome. Researchers found that these viral sequences are systematically silenced through a process called methylation.

Methylation involves chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity. It is one of the ways cells control which genetic instructions are used and which remain inactive. In this case, the ancient viral insertion appears to have caused a neighboring gene involved in brain development to be switched off.

Jakobsson notes understanding these differences in gene regulation could also provide important insights into how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.

Miniature Brains Reveal a Striking Genetic Difference.

To investigate the virus's effects, researchers grew miniature brain models called organoids using stem cells from humans and chimpanzees. These three-dimensional structures reproduce certain features of developing brain tissue, allowing scientists to study aspects of early brain development under controlled laboratory conditions.

According to recent reports, when the team compared the two types of organoids, the difference was striking. LINC00662 showed strong activity in the human brain models but was completely inactive in those derived from chimpanzee cells.

"The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids," indicates Patricia Gerdes, postdoc in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The researchers then set out to determine whether the ancient viral DNA was directly responsible for this difference.

Using CRISPR-Cas9, a powerful gene editing technology that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the viral sequence from chimpanzee cells.

The result provided compelling evidence. Once the viral DNA was removed, the previously inactive LINC00662 gene switched back on.

"This reveals that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees," says Patricia Gerdes.

Latest Clues to Human Brain Evolution.

The team also wanted to understand what LINC00662 actually does in the human brain. To investigate, they used CRISPR to switch off the gene in human brain organoids and examined how other genes responded.

According to recent reports, disabling LINC00662 reduced the activity of genes associated with nerve cell development and the formation of connections between neurons. These processes are essential for establishing the networks that allow the brain to communicate and function.

The results suggest that LINC00662 contributes to important stages of early human brain development, while the ancient viral insertion prevents the gene from functioning in chimpanzees.

More broadly, the discovery highlights an key principle of evolution. Although humans and chimpanzees share much of their genetic material, differences in how genes are switched on and off can influence how their bodies and brains develop.

The findings suggest that ancient viral infections may have contributed to these differences by altering gene regulation long after the original infections disappeared.

Researchers now strategy to investigate whether other remnants of ancient viruses have similarly influenced brain evolution. They also hope to determine whether these inherited viral sequences may play a role in neurological diseases.

Together, the discoveries raise an intriguing possibility that some of the differences between human and chimpanzee brains may trace back, at least in part, to viruses that infected our evolutionary relatives millions of years ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

In a recent development, the automaker noted Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

In a recent development, alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, mentioned licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as swiftly as possible.

Sources indicate that "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

It has been revealed that in September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Sources indicate that ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the firm's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford stated it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.
